content: A reducing sugar is defined as any sugar that, in a basic solution, is capable of forming an aldehyde or ketone group. These sugars can be obtained from reputable chemical suppliers. Examples of reducing sugars include glucose, fructose, glyceraldehyde, lactose, arabinose, and maltose. Monosaccharides that contain ketone groups are classified as ketoses, while those containing aldehyde groups are referred to as aldoses. It is important to note that sucrose is not a reducing sugar; it is classified as a non-reducing sugar. To test for the presence of a reducing sugar, Benedict's reagent is commonly used. When a reducing sugar is present, the solution changes color to green, orange, or red, depending on the concentration of the sugar. Similarly, Fehling's solution can also be employed for this purpose. Both Benedict's reagent and Fehling's solution contain copper (II) ions, which are reduced to copper (I) oxide, forming a brick-red precipitate when the solution is heated. The reducing property of a sugar is dependent on the availability of its anomeric carbon in a free form. Sugars exist in equilibrium between their chain and ring structures. In the chain form, the aldehyde or ketone group is exposed and can reduce copper (II) ions. During this reaction, the aldehyde or ketone group is oxidized to a carboxyl group.
